sentences.text: Titanohierax gloveralleni, known as the Bahama eagle, was a large extinct hawk that lived during the Late Quaternary in the Caribbean. This giant bird of prey weighed approximately 7.3 kg, a mass similar to that of female modern eagles. It possessed a front claw measuring 57 mm, making it slightly smaller than the largest known bird of prey, Haast's eagle.

The tarsometatarsus of Titanohierax is significantly larger than that of any living buteogalline, its closest relatives. Alexander Wetmore identified a partial metacarpal as belonging to Titanohierax based on its similarity to Buteogallus urubitinga and its massive size.
The extinct Buteogallus borrasi was formerly classified within the genus Titanohierax alongside T. gloveralleni.

Remains of Titanohierax have been discovered on multiple islands within the Bahamas. The first fossils were discovered in 1937 in cavern deposits on the island of Little Exuma in the Bahamas. Vivienne Knowles discovered the remains while separating them from cave earth intended for fertilizer.

Alexander Wetmore described the species in 1937 based on a tarsometatarsus and a partial metacarpal. Wetmore described the species and named it Titanohierax gloveralleni in the same year the fossils were found. Wetmore initially misidentified the location of the fossils as Great Exuma instead of Little Exuma. Max Hecht later identified the correct sites, noting that the fossiliferous soils had been removed. The holotype was likely found in Upper Pasture Cave on Little Exuma, located about fifty feet above sea level on the western side.

During the Pleistocene, Titanohierax gloveralleni was an apex predator in the Bahamas that fed on large hutias like Geocapromys. During the Pleistocene, Titanohierax served as an apex predator on the Bahaman islands.

Researchers believe habitat loss for the hawk and its prey, combined with potential human pressure, caused its extinction. Researchers suggest the extinction of Titanohierax may be linked to a decline in its preferred prey, the rodent Geocapromys. A 2018 publication by Oswald and Steadman cites the loss of preferred habitat as a possible factor in Titanohierax's extinction.

The genus Titanohierax was established by Wetmore in 1937. The type species of the genus Titanohierax is Titanohierax gloveralleni. The closest living relatives of Titanohierax gloveralleni are modern species of the genus Buteogallus.
Fossils of Titanohierax date back to the Pleistocene epoch. Titanohierax lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.

Geological and faunal evidence dated the Banana Hole site to the pre-Pamlico portion of the Wisconsin glacial stage, approximately 17,000 years old. 17,000 years ago, when Titanohierax lived, the Bahamas consisted of five major islands and several minor ones linked by lower sea levels. During the Wisconsinan glacial stage, temperatures on the islands were up to 4 degrees Celsius lower than today.

In 2004, William Suárez refuted the assignment of Aquila borrasi to Titanohierax, concluding it was a valid species but belonged to a different genus. It is debated whether the post-glacial decrease in Caribbean island size substantially contributed to Titanohierax's extinction, with some researchers arguing it did not.
